political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Joyce's 'The End of Social History?' (1995; unread) drew their 'Starting Over' (1995; unread), which Joyce said equated his questioning of social history 'with contemporary neo-liberalism' (1996). The debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.

environment.label: Environmental history
environment.date_label: 1970s consolidation · Environmental History (journal) 1996 · NiCHE 2004 · Canadian number of Environmental History 2007 · Sutter forum 2013 · Oxford Handbook 2014 · reviewed through 2024
environment.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature; the approaches disagree about causal emphasis, and cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecology with power without one model. Bullard and the Huggins life histories add unequal burdens and authority over accounts; the Dust Bowl debates set capitalism, technology, policy and survival against one another. After 1995 the field argued with itself and its neighbours: Cronon called wilderness 'quite profoundly a human creation'; Foreman answered that this 'Received Wilderness Idea is a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground' (2000); Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks. A merged journal (1996), McNeill's world synthesis (2000) and a Canadian network (NiCHE, 2004) widened it; by 2013 Sutter found nature and culture replaced by 'environmental hybridity' (editors' summary). Chakrabarty (2009) and the Anthropocene histories of 2016 set its questions at planetary scale.
environment.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history. After 2000: J. R. McNeill, Something New Under the Sun (2000) and 'Observations' (2003); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Sutter, 'The World with Us' (JAH 2013); Isenberg, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Environmental History (2014); in Canada, Wynn (series editor), MacEachern, Loo, Piper, Sandlos, Evenden, Colpitts, Parr; the Anthropocene: Chakrabarty (2009), McNeill and Engelke, Malm, Bonneuil and Fressoz (2016). Institutions: Environmental History (journal, 1996), NiCHE (2004).

Books unread here. He answered Cronon's wilderness essay in the first number of Environmental History (1996): 'Cronon's wilderness is a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (as quoted by Foreman, 2000; the comment itself unread).

environment.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community. Extended to 2024 on 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md). Read in full: Foreman's 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000), Cronon's CV and 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003), the NiCHE and UBC Press series pages, publisher pages and abstracts for the Canadian books and articles, two open reviews of Worster's Shrinking the Earth; passages read: Cronon's 'Storytelling' (2013) and McNeill's AHA address (2020). Unread: the 1996 comments by Hays, Cohen and Dunlap and Cronon's response; Sutter's 2013 essay and its six responses (the editors' summary is quoted instead); McNeill 2000 and 2003 (the latter known from the earlier record); the 2005 'What's Next' forum including Linda Nash on agency; the bodies of every Canadian book; Malm, Moore, Bonneuil and Fressoz beyond descriptions. The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 dates the field's readership: 1.6% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of its authors in the 1990s, 5.7% in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25; the network of works co-cited with its founders (Cronon's Changes, Nature's Metropolis and 'The Trouble with Wilderness'; Worster's Dust Bowl, Rivers of Empire and Nature's Economy; White's Organic Machine; Crosby's Ecological Imperialism; Merchant's Death of Nature; works with lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 (37 works) and halved by 2020–25 (17), its new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; in the US it is stable (17–19 works) and its entrants are Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. The History PhD citation graph interprets these sampled co-citation neighbourhoods as diffusion into neighbouring historiographies. This does not establish declining scholarly production or the field's own understanding of its development.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.
strands.works: Dust Bowl (1979); “The Dirty Thirties” (1986)

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980)

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.
strands.works: This Fissured Land (1992)

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.
strands.works: “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995; journal reprint with comments and a response, Environmental History 1:1, January 1996)

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.
strands.works: History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994), 14 September readings

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.
strands.works: Malin (1946,1950), critically discussed by Worster (1986)

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.
strands.works: McDean (1986); Fite (1983); Rooted in Dust (1994)

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.
strands.works: Guha (1989); Cronon (1995), including note 28

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.
strands.works: Guha (1989); Johns (1990), abstract

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.
strands.works: Cronon (1995); Sessions (1996)

strands.title: Material change, ideas and gendered nature
strands.focus: Merchant retrospectively clarifies that ecological and economic changes made some ideas more plausible rather than mechanically causing them. Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction and challenges an essentialist identification of women with nature.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); Radical Ecology (1992), discussed in Merchant’s 2006 retrospective

strands.title: Colonial conservation: knowledge, power and benefits
strands.focus: Carruthers’s review welcomes Grove’s island settings and exchanges of knowledge, while questioning parts of his synthesis. Her Kruger prologue and epilogue emphasize changing political coalitions, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Scientific conservation and unequal power can coexist; these works ask different questions at different scales.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

strands.title: The wilderness debate, 1995–2000: a selected exchange
strands.focus: Cronon's essay (1995; reprinted with comments in the first number of Environmental History, January 1996) held wilderness to be 'quite profoundly a human creation' and 'a flight from history' while defending wild-land protection. Hays replied in the journal that 'Cronon's wilderness is a world of abstracted ideas … divorced from the values and ideas inherent in wilderness action' (as quoted by Foreman; comment unread). Sessions objected from conservation biology (1996). Callicott and Nelson gathered thirty-nine essays as The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998), where Foreman's 'Wilderness Areas for Real' answered. Foreman then told a federal wilderness-science conference (1999; printed 2000) that he came 'not to praise The Received Wilderness Idea, but to bury it': the idea that 'Baird Callicott, Bill Cronon and other postmodern deconstructionist scholars so eagerly banish' was 'a straw dog; it does not exist on the ground', unlike 'the Real Wilderness Idea' that built the National Wilderness Preservation System. A selected exchange: Cohen's and Dunlap's comments, the editors' introduction to the anthology and Cronon's 1996 response (pp. 47–55) are unread; in 2003 he answered in practice, asking that the Apostle Islands be managed 'as a historical wilderness' — 'Emphatically yes' to designation, but 'a storied wilderness'.
strands.works: 'The Trouble with Wilderness' (1995; Environmental History 1:1, 1996, with comments and a response); Callicott and Nelson, eds., The Great New Wilderness Debate (1998); Foreman, 'The Real Wilderness Idea' (2000); Cronon, 'The Riddle of the Apostle Islands' (2003)

strands.title: The Anthropocene and the climate of history
strands.focus: Chakrabarty's four theses (2009) held that anthropogenic climate change collapses the distinction between natural and human history (edge_918; critics at edge_1147). Environmental historians then wrote the epoch: McNeill and Engelke's The Great Acceleration (2016) says 'The Earth has entered a new age—the Anthropocene' and that 'human dependence on fossil fuels inaugurated' it; Malm's Fossil Capital (2016) answers that 'steam offered neither cheaper nor more abundant energy' but control over labour, against what a reviewer on its cover calls the 'Anthropocene narrative'; Bonneuil and Fressoz refuse 'the convenient view of a "human species" that upset the Earth system, unaware of what it was doing' (publisher descriptions; bodies unread). Worster's Shrinking the Earth (2016) was read by Collomb as 'reflections of the greatest US environmental historian on humankind's future and the Anthropocene'. McNeill told the AHA (2020) that 'environmental history stands to be disrupted, and with luck enhanced, more than most fields'. In PhD bibliographies this is a strand of the historiography, not of reading: Chakrabarty is cited by 4.5% of Canada + US theses in 2020–25, in three families (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).
strands.works: Chakrabarty, 'The Climate of History' (2009); McNeill and Engelke, The Great Acceleration (2016); Malm, Fossil Capital (2016); Bonneuil and Fressoz, The Shock of the Anthropocene (2016); Worster, Shrinking the Earth (2016)

strands.title: Canadian environmental history: a network and a series, 2001–2019
strands.focus: Wynn (2003) found the field 'undeveloped in this country, compared with the United States'. Within a decade it had institutions: NiCHE, 'founded in fall 2004 by a small team of scholars' and funded by a SSHRC Strategic Knowledge Cluster grant from 2007 (MacEachern director; Wynn, Turkel, Castonguay, Evenden and Piper on the executive); Wynn's UBC Press series Nature | History | Society, 'devoted to the publication of high-quality scholarship in environmental history and allied fields'; and a Canadian number of Environmental History (October 2007, edited by Evenden and MacEachern) in which Piper and Sandlos found that 'the Canadian North was never subject to the broad ecological transformation that occurred further to the south' and Loo argued that environmental justice 'requires coming to terms with the different scales' at which change is apprehended. The books — MacEachern on Atlantic parks (2001), Evenden on the Fraser (2004), Loo on wildlife (2006), Sandlos on northern game laws (2007), Piper on subarctic industry (2009), Parr on the senses (2010), Colpitts on pemmican (2014), Loo on relocation (2019) — won the CHA's prizes and, in Canadian PhD bibliographies, entered the company of Cronon, Worster and White in 2010–19 (MacEachern and Loo in 2010–14; Parr, Piper, Evenden and Sandlos in 2015–19; History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23). Loo (2014) asked the field to 'use more of the world, and vice versa'.
strands.works: NiCHE (2004); Nature | History | Society (UBC Press); Environmental History 12:4 (2007); MacEachern (2001), Evenden (2004), Loo (2006, 2019), Sandlos (2007), Piper (2009), Parr (2010), Colpitts (2014); Loo, 'Missed Connections' (2014)

strands.title: Conservation, dispossession and neighbouring historiographies
strands.focus: Cronon wrote that 'The removal of Indians to create an "uninhabited wilderness"' showed 'just how invented, just how constructed, the American wilderness really is' (1995). Spence (1999) examined Indian removal in the making of national parks: Dispossessing the Wilderness traced how 'the early conception of the wilderness as the place where Indians lived (or should live)' gave way to 'the idealization of uninhabited wilderness' at Yellowstone, Glacier and Yosemite. Warren's The Hunter's Game (1997) and Jacoby's Crimes against Nature (2001; Marsh and Littleton-Griswold prizes), by Cronon's doctoral students, wrote the social history of poaching and conservation (unread; no reader read here links them to the wilderness essay). In Canada, Binnema and Niemi (2006) argued that the Stoney were excluded from Banff for game conservation, sport hunting, tourism and assimilation rather than for a wilderness ideal, and Sandlos (2007) that game laws and sanctuaries 'helped the state assert authority over traditional hunting cultures'; Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), with disease and climate among its causes, is blurbed by McNeill and read with Wolfe. The dissertation record records an associated readership pattern: the works newly co-cited with the field's founders after 2015 are Wolfe, Tuck and Yang, The Middle Ground, Hämäläinen, DuVal and O'Brien (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23; founders Cronon ×3, Worster ×3, White, Crosby, Merchant; lift ≥ 3; averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses). Settler colonial studies is its own entry; the link between the two is drawn there.
strands.works: Warren, The Hunter's Game (1997); Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Jacoby, Crimes against Nature (2001); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007); Daschuk, Clearing the Plains (2013)

The History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23 gives the readership: 5.7% of Canada + US theses cited two or more of the field's authors in 2000–09, 9.5% in 2010–14, 11.3% in 2015–19, 9.9% in 2020–25 (Canada 10.2%, US 9.7%); the works co-cited with nine founding titles by Cronon, Worster, White, Crosby and Merchant (lift ≥ 3, averaged over repeated samples of fifteen seed-citing theses) peaked in Canada in 2010–14 and halved by 2020–25, the new members being Wolfe and Tuck and Yang; the US network is stable in size, its entrants Indigenous, borderlands and slavery works. post.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.

science.label: History of science
science.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches
science.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.

urbanhistory.date_label: Earlier city histories · postwar expansion · Urban History Yearbook 1974
urbanhistory.description: Studies cities and urbanization through institutions, populations, built environments and connections beyond city boundaries. Local reconstruction, quantitative mobility research, colonial spatial analysis and histories of segregation or public landscapes form different approaches.
urbanhistory.representative_figures_and_works: H. J. Dyos: Urban History Yearbook programme (1974); Sam Bass Warner Jr.: Streetcar Suburbs (1962; second edition 1978); Stephan Thernstrom: Poverty and Progress (1964); Thomas J. King: Colonial Urban Development (1976); William Cronon: Nature’s Metropolis (1991); Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Lynn Hollen Lees: “The challenge of political change” (1994). David Harvey: Social Justice and the City (1973); Walter Benjamin: Das Passagen-Werk (1982); Michel de Certeau: “Walking in the City” (1980). Sven Beckert, The Monied Metropolis (2001), selected introduction on urban bourgeois class formation.

urbanhistory.scope_note: British institution-building and US quantitative urban studies do not define one school or exhaust the field. Cities are not self-contained units. Delhi adds a specific colonial inquiry; wider Asian, African, Latin American and medieval/early-modern historiographies remain underrepresented. Journal milestones mark consolidation, not the first historical study of cities.

strands.title: Urban elites and the formation of a bourgeoisie
strands.focus: Beckert makes the coherence of New York’s capital-owning elites a historical question. Institutions, cultural boundaries and political conflicts help explain how a shared class identity was made. This selected introduction adds an urban elite-formation problem alongside existing histories of neighbourhoods, mobility and racial inequality; it does not replace them.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.

Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.
